chapters.summary: Council staff opens the Committee on Contracts hearing, announces that no one may approach the dais, directs testifiers to the Sergeant at Arms, prohibits food and drinks, and invites Chair Restler to begin.
chapters.title: Council staff opens hearing and announces rules

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good afternoon and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing on Committee on Contracts.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, during today's hearing, no one may approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you would like to testify, please find surgeon at arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: No food or drinks allowed.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Chair Lincoln Restler opens the hearing, acknowledges Councilmembers Hanks and Wilson, and announces the topic: PASSPort, the city's procurement and sourcing solutions portal.
chapters.title: Chair Restler opens PASSPort oversight hearing

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thanks so much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: My name is Lincoln Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I have the privilege of chairing our contracts committee.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'd like to acknowledge the attendance of our majority whip from the North Shore, Councilmember Hanks, and the newest member of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Until that changes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Friend from the West Village, Carl Wilson.

chapters.summary: Restler describes PASSPort's 2017 launch to replace paper-based VENDEX, its promise as a user-friendly tool to reduce contracting time and improve transparency, and its current coverage of the procurement lifecycle.
chapters.title: Restler outlines PASSPort history and promises

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Today's hearing is about Passport, the procurement and sourcing solutions portal.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If you didn't know Passport was short for something, it is.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The system, this system the city uses to run its procurement.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And whether it's giving agencies, vendors, or this council the information we need to make contracting work, we all depend on Passport every single day.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The city launched Passport in 2017 as an end-to-end procurement platform to replace the city's paper-based VENDEX system.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just want to say that again because it's less than a decade ago that we were relying on a paper-based VENDEX system.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: With over $30 billion in procurement every single year, this was a monumental step.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: To bringing our contracting system into the 21st century.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Passport was promised to be a user-friendly online tool to reduce the time needed to do business with the city and improve transparency.

chapters.summary: Restler notes $36.6B in FY26 procurement across 209,000 transactions, at least $120M spent on PASSPort maintenance and upgrades, and continued delays in registration, budget approvals, and invoicing, especially for nonprofits.
chapters.title: Restler details PASSPort spending and persistent delays

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Passport now covers the entire life cycle of city procurements, from solicitations to awards to payments.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2026, the city procured about 36

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: $6 billion in goods and services through more than 209,000 transactions, and Passport is where the record of that spending lives.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: While Passport has unquestionably been an upgrade from a paper-based system, nine years and six updates later, questions remain on whether this is the best system to continue to meet our contracting goals.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The city has spent at least $120 million on passport maintenance contracts and upgrades over the past 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yet on-time processing of registration, budget approvals, invoicing, it all continues to fall far below our collective standards, especially as it relates to the nonprofit sector.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And Passport has not offered the transparency or the insights we hoped it would in pinpointing exactly where those delays are happening.

chapters.summary: Restler shares that nonprofits report taking half a day to submit a single invoice, agencies say the system creates administrative work, and the city does not own the software, making improvements hard and expensive.
chapters.title: Restler describes nonprofit and agency frustrations with PASSPort

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Many nonprofits and city agencies have also continued to struggle with Passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We've heard ongoing frustrations with the technology limitations and glitches.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: One nonprofit shared that it takes them half a day.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Of work, half a day of work, to upload and submit a single invoice.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Time that should be spent on delivering services for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: City agencies have also reported that this clunky system leads to unnecessary administrative work instead of streamlining their processes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In short, in Passport,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We have an inefficient system that nobody likes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We do not own the software, and upgrades are not...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: not caply eligible.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So improvements are hard to achieve and quite expensive.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But with tens of billions of dollars in annual contract spending, vendors and city agencies alike deserve a system that works better.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: As we look to the future of procurement in New York City, I hope to gain a better understanding today of how MOX is evaluating

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: the performance of Passport, and what options are on the table moving forward.

chapters.summary: Restler previews Intro 991 on standard designs, Intro 1064 on approval and change-order timeframes, Intro 1065 on cost benchmarks, and Reso 619 on lowering the design-build threshold, naming sponsors Banks, Wilson, Williams, and Dinowitz.
chapters.title: Restler introduces four small-capital-project bills and Reso 619

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We will also hear four pieces of legislation today that all are aimed at making small capital projects faster, cheaper, and more predictable.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Intro 991, sponsored by Councilmember Banks, would require...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Deputy Leader, did I have that right?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I can't, I'm struggling on titles.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Deputy Leader Banks would require DDC to create a catalog of standard pre-approved designs for small capital structures like park restrooms, field houses, storage buildings.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Intro 1064, sponsored by Councilmember Wilson, would require DDC to set timeframes for agencies to act on approvals and change orders on capital projects of $10 million or less.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Intro 1065, also sponsored by Councilmember Williams, would require DDC to set cost benchmarks for each type of small capital structure based on what those projects actually cost.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And Reso 619, sponsored by Councilmember Dinowitz, calls on the state to lower the dollar threshold for design-build.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Right now, most city agencies can only use design-build on projects of $10 million or more.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Which leaves out small projects that these bills are aimed at.

chapters.summary: Restler thanks Councilmember Vernikov for joining and recognizes contracts committee staff Alex Polanoff, Alex Yablon, and Andrew Lane Lawless before turning to Councilmember Wilson.
chapters.title: Restler thanks members and committee staff

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I want to thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank Councilmember Bernikov, my neighbor in Brooklyn, for joining.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And before we begin, I'd really like to just thank the team that does all the work to make these hearings possible, our distinguished contracts committee staff,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: senior legislative counsel Alex Polanoff, legislative policy analyst Alex Yablon, and principal financial analyst Andrew Lane Lawless.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: With that, I am going to turn it over to Council Member Carl Wilson to say a few words.

chapters.summary: Carl Wilson says capital projects often go over budget and time without oversight, and introduces his legislation to set cost benchmarks and timeframes for small capital projects.
chapters.title: Councilmember Wilson introduces his small-capital-project bills

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Too often, capital projects go massively over budget and over time for no clear reason and with little proper oversight.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: The legislation I'm proposing today aims to establish cost benchmarks and timeframes for small capital projects, as the chair alluded to.

chapters.summary: Wilson says Intro 1065 would require DDC to publish cost benchmarks for small capital structures up to 2,500 square feet, report annually on actual costs, and reassess benchmarks.
chapters.title: Wilson explains Intro 1065 cost benchmarks

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Intro 1065 would require DDC to publish cost benchmarks for each type of small capital structure defined as freestanding buildings up to 2,500 square feet, such as bathrooms and field houses.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: The department would have to submit reports every year on the difference between those benchmarks and the actual cost of such projects and would regularly reassess the cost benchmarks they put forward.

chapters.summary: Wilson says Intro 1064 would require DDC to consult MOCS and agencies to set timeframes for approvals and change orders on projects $10M and under, with delay explanations and new timeframes if missed.
chapters.title: Wilson explains Intro 1064 approval timeframes

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Intro 1064 would require DDC to consult with the Mayor's Office of Contract Services and other relevant agencies to establish timeframes for completing agency approvals and change order requests from contractors regarding capital projects costs.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: costing $10 million and under.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: If the timeframe is not met, the relevant agency must explain the reason for the delay within 10 days and provide a new approval timeframe.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: These bills will establish some much needed chronological and financial uniformity when it comes to small capital projects and will help inform the public too.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: For example, the annual reports on compliance with cost benchmarks would be posted on the DDC's website, as would timeframes for agency approvals and change orders.

chapters.summary: Wilson thanks colleagues who co-sponsored the bills, including Parks Chair Hankerson and Contracts Chair Restler, and appreciates the committee's consideration.
chapters.title: Wilson thanks co-sponsors and committee

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So thank you to my colleagues who have co-sponsored these bills, including Parks Committee Chair Hankerson.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: For sponsoring intros 1064 and 65.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And of course, the contract committee chair, Ressler, for co-sponsoring 1064.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I appreciate the contracts committee consideration of these bills today.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Restler thanks Councilmember Stevens, praises her advocacy on contracts and nonprofits, and designates her vice chair of the Contracts Committee.
chapters.title: Restler recognizes Stevens as contracts vice chair

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Williams.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I am especially excited to recognize the presence of my colleague, Councilmember Stevens, whose

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: passion and commitment to the contracts committee has led to the new designation of vice chair of the contracts committee.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And unless the speaker tells me that I'm not allowed to do this, we're going to make this permanent.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I want to thank her for joining us today and for her.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Really for her impassioned and thoughtful advocacy on contracts issues, especially as it relates to the nonprofit sector.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It really makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I don't think she cares either.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's why it's going to be permanent.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Vice Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Stevens from here on out.

chapters.summary: Restler thanks Councilmember Gennaro on Zoom and welcomes Commissioner Ochoa and Director Yu; committee staff swears in administration witnesses.
chapters.title: Committee swears in administration witnesses

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: With that, I want to thank Councilmember Gennaro, who's on Zoom, and I really want to thank Commissioner Ochoa and Director Yu for joining us today, and I'll invite the Committee Council to swear in our witnesses.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Will all members of the administration testifying today please raise your right hands?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you swear or affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your testimony today and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin when ready.

chapters.summary: Kim Yu, chief procurement officer and MOCS director, thanks the committee and says she will discuss PASSPort's evolution, role in city contracting, and efforts to improve agency, business, and nonprofit experience.
chapters.title: Kim Yu introduces herself and frames PASSPort testimony

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Ressler, Vice Chair Stevens, Majority Whip Hanks, Council Member Vernikov, and Council Member Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And Councilmember Gennaro.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I'm Kim Yu, the city's chief procurement officer and the director of the mayor's office of contract services.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Thank you for your continued engagement and the opportunity to discuss how Passport has evolved, its role in city contracting today, and our work to improve the experience of the agencies, businesses, and nonprofit providers that rely on it.

chapters.summary: Yu describes paper submissions, manual data entry, and separate systems before PASSPort, and says the goal was a shared digital environment with greater continuity and visibility.
chapters.title: Yu recounts pre-PASSPort contracting challenges and goals

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The story of Passport begins with a challenge familiar to anyone who has worked through a complicated government process.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Completing one step did not necessarily make it easier to reach the next.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Before Passport, city contracting depended on paper submissions, manual data entry, and separate systems that supported different activities.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: These are

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Arrangements made contracting labor-intensive and limited the city's ability to identify where work was delayed and why.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Passport was developed to bring those activities into a shared digital environment and create greater continuity across the contracting processes.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The goal was to make it possible for information and work to move from one stage to the next with greater visibility for everyone involved.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: A business seeking a city contract needed a clearer path from finding an opportunity to submitting a proposal and completing its contracting requirements.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Agency staff needed tools to manage reviews and approvals, and oversight offices needed a more complete picture of how procurements were progressing.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Building a platform to serve those different needs required changes to both the technology and the way people carried out their work.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: That transition took place in phases.

chapters.summary: Yu says PASSPort replaced VENDEX forms in 2017, added purchasing and competitive bids, handled full procurement by 2020, and later absorbed Human Services financial activities from HHS Accelerator.
chapters.title: Yu outlines PASSPort rollout and HHS Accelerator migration

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: In 2017, the city replaced paper-based Vendex forms with an online system where vendors could enter and update their own information.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Later releases added purchasing tools and support for competitive bids.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: By 2020, agencies could handle the full process, from posting opportunities to preparing contracts within Passport, and veterans could respond and complete the steps needed for registration.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: When Mox last testified before this committee in February 2020,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: 2022, we were expanding the platform's financial functions.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Since that hearing, Passport has taken on a larger role in the ongoing management of city contracts.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Human Services financial activities previously managed in HHS Accelerator moved into the platform with added functionality that traveled throughout the life of a contract.

chapters.summary: Yu says scaling PASSPort brought new challenges and limitations into focus, and that Release 7 is intended to remove significant barriers for agencies and vendors.
chapters.title: Yu acknowledges platform limitations and Release 7 focus

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: This growth has also brought the platform's limitation into sharper focus.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Bringing activities into one system creates greater visibility, but with any scaling, it brings new challenges as we work out how providers are interacting with the system.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Our focus today is on how we are responding to those experiences.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The upcoming Release 7 is intended to remove significant barriers, and we are focusing on making the platform more effective in the daily work of the agencies and the vendors that depend on it.

chapters.summary: Yu reports more than 87,000 active users in the prior year, including 31,000 agency users and 59,000 vendor users, and describes benefits for agencies, vendors, and MOCS monitoring.
chapters.title: Yu presents PASSPort user and transaction statistics

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: As of October 23, 2026, more than 87,000 users across city agencies and the vendor community had been active on the platform over the preceding year.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Including more than 31,000 agency users and 59,000 vendor users.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: For agencies, a shared system provides greater visibility into contracting activities and the reviews they require.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: For vendors, it provides a place to respond to opportunities, maintain required information, and manage contracts and financial tasks.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: For MOX, it supports monitoring across agencies and help inform conversation.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: about performance and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The platform must also accommodate a wide range of procurement methods, contract types, financial activities, and oversight requirements.

chapters.summary: Yu says Release 7 will allow invoice submission and financial actions to proceed while eligible budget and funding changes are underway, with safeguards and a new financial activities view.
chapters.title: Yu details Release 7 financial workflow improvements

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Release 7 tackles a common issue in Passport.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Work often gets held up because of one financial task blocks another.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Agencies regularly need to update funding, adjust budgets, and process invoices.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But the current system can force these activities to wait, causing avoidable delays.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: MOX has already reduced some payment delays by directing agencies to use partial payments so providers can be paid for approved costs while other items are still being resolved.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Release 7 addresses delays that occur even earlier by allowing invoice submission and other financial actions to proceed while eligible budget and funding changes are underway.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Supported by safeguards to ensure funding is available.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The release also adds clearer guardrails on a new ongoing financial activities view, so users can see what work is in progress and avoid conflicts, helping financial tasks move forward more smoothly.

chapters.summary: Yu says the release plan includes testing with agency users, updated training materials, and preparing support staff to identify problems before deployment and maintain contracting continuity.
chapters.title: Yu describes Release 7 implementation and training

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Preparing users for these changes is an essential part of implementation.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The Release 7 plan includes testing with agency users, development of updated training materials, and preparation of the staff who will support the new workflows.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: That work is intended to identify problems before deployment and help agencies and vendors understand how their responsibilities

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Our implementation approach must account for the continuity of contracting and payment activities throughout the transition.

chapters.summary: Yu says MOCS introduced vendor reporting for direct access to sourcing, contract, and financial data, and reduced average service desk resolution time from 21 days in 2025 to eight days in 2026.
chapters.title: Yu discusses vendor reporting and service desk improvements

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: In response to the feedback we collect from both our smaller and larger organizations, MOX introduced vendor reporting, which gives vendors direct access to their sourcing, contract, and financial data within Passport.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And helps with their day-to-day management.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Direct assistance remains equally important.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The MOC service desk supports agency staff and vendors who encounter technical problems, need help understanding a requirement, or are unsure how to complete a task.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Those requests vary in complexity, but each represents someone trying to move work forward.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Mox has made progress in improving service desk performance.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: As of October 22, 2026, average resolution times was eight days, down from 21 days in 2025, a reduction of approximately 63%.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The service desk had received more than 16,000 requests this year.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: These improvements help reduce the time users spend waiting for assistance and allow them to return more quickly to the contracting and financial tasks they need to complete.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Sustaining that progress requires continued attention to the quality of the response, the complexity of the outstanding requests, and whether the assistance provided results.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Resolves the underlying problem.

chapters.summary: Yu says service desk requests reveal training and technical needs, and MOCS uses webinars, workshops, and written resources; near-term priorities include transparency, provider readiness, timely registration, and Release 7 preparation.
chapters.title: Yu describes training resources and near-term priorities

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Service desk requests also provide valuable information about the platform itself.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Repeated questions about the same activity can point to unclear instructions, a training need, or technical issues.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Through MOX Institute, virtual and in-person sessions, vendor workshops, and written resources, MOX helps users build the knowledge needed to navigate city procurement.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The Getting Started webinar series provides demonstrations of passport functions and opportunities to ask questions, while Mocks in Your Neighborhood helps businesses and community-based organizations better understand how to do business with the city.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Our near-term focus is clear.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We are continuing to improve procurement transparency through vendor reporting,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: strengthen provider readiness through our budget readiness work, improve contract registration performance through our timely registration efforts, and prepare agencies and vendors for Passport Release 7.

chapters.summary: Yu says the procurement system connects billions in public funding to services and shapes economic opportunity, and MOCS remains committed to reliability, transparency, and integrity with Council partnership.
chapters.title: Yu closes with commitment to procurement system improvement

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: New York City's procurement system connects billions of dollars in public funding to the services and infrastructure residents rely on every day.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It also shapes economic opportunity for businesses and nonprofit organizations across the city.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Making that system work requires sustained planning, strategy, execution, and oversight.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Technology is an essential part of that capacity.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Together with clear rules, knowledgeable staff, and coordination among the agencies and partners responsible for moving contracts forward.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The measure of our progress is whether those elements work together to help agencies deliver effectively

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: and allow providers to operate with greater certainty.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: MOX remains committed to improving the reliability, transparency, and integrity of the city's procurement system.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We appreciate the Council's continued partnership and focus on these issues, and we look forward to working together to make the city's contracting system more effective for agencies, providers, businesses, and the New Yorkers they serve.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I look forward to your questions.

chapters.summary: Ochoa says DDC has had success with design-build, CM-build, and progressive design-build, and asks the Council to advocate for long-term or permanent extension of the Public Works Investment Act before it expires December 31, 2027.
chapters.title: Ochoa addresses Reso 619 and PWIA extensions

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I've had the privilege of spending these past few months getting to know the dedicated architects, engineers, and project managers at DDC, as well as every sponsor agency that we work with, including the libraries and every other agency.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Let me start by addressing the resolution being heard today, Resolution 619, to amend the New York City Public Works Investment Act.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We have seen tremendous success in alternative delivery tools, design-built, CM-built, and progressive design-built.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We appreciate any support the Council can provide with our Albany colleagues on advocating for long-term extensions for the public works.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Investment Act.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: This is the umbrella organization that approves both of these tools.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: This coming session is when we're going to be asking for your help.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Both of these tools expire December 31st, 2027.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I've said this before, I'm going to have a much easier job than my DDC predecessors in making the argument for renewal since we already have proof of concepts that these tools work.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: To put our request clearly, we need PWIA extended long-term or permanently without restrictions, including no limitations on CM-built project types, which are currently only permitted for libraries and cultural institutions.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I would be happy to share additional thoughts on design-build projects and the threshold in Q&A.

chapters.summary: Ochoa agrees on standardizing small capital structures but says every building is unique due to user requirements, square footage, location, technology, and code upgrades, making standard designs difficult.
chapters.title: Ochoa responds to Intro 991 on standard designs

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Now on to the bills being heard today.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Introduction 991 requiring a catalog of standard design for small recurring capital projects.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We agree on the importance of standardizing the design of small capital structures like boilers, roof replacements, and facades, which are vital for public buildings and their service to the public.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We have worked with our sponsors to streamline the design.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Building designs, i.e.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Parks, recreation centers, FDNY, EMS stations, DSNY garages.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: The reality is that every building, even new ones with the set criteria, are unique based on the front-end user requirements, the square footage, and the location.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: For example, the design of a boiler we installed last year will not be the same for another boiler installation two years based on new technology and code requirement upgrades.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I'm happy to discuss further.

chapters.summary: Ochoa says change orders are challenging, DDC uses expanded work allowance to pay vendors partially, and the process involves negotiation, engineering audit, amended CPs, and controller registration; no two change orders are the same.
chapters.title: Ochoa responds to Intro 1064 on change-order timeframes

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Intro 1064, timeframes for agency approvals and change order on small.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Every capital agency recognizes that change orders are challenging and are paying vendors is essential to keeping projects moving,

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: ensuring our union labors are paid and avoid placing undue financial burdens on the industry partners who front the money to keep the projects moving.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: DDC was the first agency to use expanded work allowance, EWA.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Additional registered contingency from OMB at the beginning of a project that allows us to pay vendors, at least partially, while we finalize the change order process.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: EWA has now been expanded to all DDC projects, and we're looking at ways to add something similar for design contracts.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: The change order process itself can be challenging.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Once an unforeseen field condition is identified, we negotiate with the vendor.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Before a payment is processed, our engineering audit office, EAO, ensures that the costs are reasonable and fully above board.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: If the change order leads us to exceed our certificate to proceed cost, essentially the budgeted amount that we have transferred from OMB to spend on the project,

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We must seek an amended CP from OMB.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: On top of that, all change orders require registration with the controller before they can be paid out.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: While we understand the purpose of the timeline and report, like the standard design bill, no two change orders are the same.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Regarding notifications to contractors, project managers and field staff already keep contractors aware.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Of where they are in the process.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: At DDC, we have worked closely with stakeholders to improve the efficiency of our payment processes, including the elimination of several forms and notary requirements.

chapters.summary: Ochoa says DDC reviews estimated costs using historical trends, but actual benchmarks are set by the market; he welcomes continued dialogue and Council support for alternative delivery legislation.
chapters.title: Ochoa responds to Intro 1065 on cost benchmarks

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Introduction 1065, requiring cost benchmarks for all recurring capital projects.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Before any project is officially accepted by DDC from our sponsors, the project includes a thorough review by our front-end planning team to determine the estimated cost of the total project based on historical trends and factors.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We set standards on costs, but ultimately the benchmark for actual costs is set by the market.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We look forward to a continuous dialogue on the capital process and the council support for the alternative delivery legislation extension in Albany.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Thank you again for this opportunity to testify, and we welcome any questions you may have.

chapters.summary: Restler thanks both witnesses and announces question order: Majority Whip Hanks, Vice Chair Stevens, then Councilmember Wilson.
chapters.title: Restler sets Q&A order

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much to both of you for your thoughtful testimony.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We will begin with our majority whip, followed by our vice chair, followed by Councilmember Williams.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Wilson, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Jesus Christ.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's been a long day.

chapters.summary: Majority Whip Hanks says nonprofits are frustrated and may give up, cites the comptroller's report on upload problems and repeated data entry, and asks what data shows about where smaller and first-time applicants get stuck.
chapters.title: Hanks asks about nonprofit PASSPort frustrations and smaller applicants

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And committee staff.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So nonprofits have raised real frustrations.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: I used to run a not-for-profit, so I absolutely understand the frustration with Passport.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: You know, we're trying to feed families, we're trying to run youth programs, provide job training, and a lot of these organizations feel neglected.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And I worry that organizations may give up.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Before they bring an opportunity to our neighborhoods, which means, you know, they are required by contract to do the work, and the city doesn't pay them in time, and they may not be very big, so we're not, they're not,

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: able to stay small and wait on their payments.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So how do we make this process easier to use?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: The controller described in his April 2025 report of upload problems and repeated data entries.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: I worry that groups without technical staff or enough language support may be left behind.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: What are you seeing in the data?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So that's my question.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So what are you seeing in the data about where smaller and first-time applicants get stuck or stop applying?

chapters.summary: Yu highlights the discretionary grant pilot for agreements $25,000 and below, says it streamlines steps and speeds funding, and acknowledges newer procurement entrants need more support and resources.
chapters.title: Yu answers Hanks on grant pilot and support for newer providers

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Majority Whip Hanks, thank you so much for lifting this up.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I'm going to take a moment to scale out from Passport just a moment because the Mayor's Office of Contract Services is so much more than just overseeing this technology project.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And I will zoom in and talk about the Passport, the concerns that you raise.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: One, just to sort of hone in on what you're raising about the smaller nonprofit organizations or maybe the community-based organizations,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: something that I'm very, very excited to do in collaboration with the city council is the expansion of the discretionary grant pilot.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We are in year two of it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Chair Ressler and Speaker Menon was there with Mayor Mamdani when we announced that we would be scaling the pilot from year one, which was last fiscal year, to year two, this current fiscal year.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We are very, very hopeful of...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Taking a group of these smaller city council agreements, $25,000 and below, and not treating them as traditional procurements.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And we've re-engineered the process, and we're going to be treating them as grants.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And what that means is we are treating them in a more streamlined process, and we are eliminating steps in the process.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And most importantly, we are...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Able to

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: have city funding go to these organizations quicker than we've traditionally been able to.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The other benefit of this is taking these, this group of agreements

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: and not putting them in the traditional procurement process means that we've historically seen that these types of agreements are the ones that bog our city agencies down and create the backlog.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And, you know, the nonprofit provider starts the services and it's months.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Sometimes years before the funding catches up.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So not only are we having that group go faster and the funds to the organizations with less steps, but we are preventing them from clogging the system, as we like to say,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: because these are relatively low dollar amounts on these particular agreements and they are

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But the number of them is very great that we can see in the data.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And so we're very hopeful to come back in December, January, and speak about that grant pilot.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But majority with PANKS, I think I want to also address the concern around passport because that's what we're here to talk about.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: What we do see is that the newer entrants to the procurement ecosystem, they do need a little bit more support and resources than our

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: larger organizations that have been doing business with the city of New York for years and years.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And so that's why we use lots of modalities to get to them, because it is about the technology, but it's also around the resources that are available on the technology.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And it's also having folks who are on the other side, whether it's at MOX or the city agencies, who are knowledgeable about the processes and knowledgeable about the technology.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And certainly we can sort of hone in on your particular question about, like, what's the data showing us on the newer organizations.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We're happy to do that and follow up.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Well, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: You answered all my questions and the ones after that.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So thank you very much, Chair.

chapters.summary: Vice Chair Stevens praises the after-school RFP rollout but says providers cannot tell where they are in the process when the contract status bubble is inaccurate, and asks what improvements MOCS is making.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about PASSPort improvements and contract status visibility

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I will now pass it on to the vice chair of the contracts committee, Councilmember Stevens.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Chair Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I guess you did make fetch happen because he's been calling me his vice chair since he got this committee.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But in all seriousness, I'm really happy to see you here, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And as you know, I'm super passionate about this.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And one, I want to give you a shout out and a kudos because we were very worried about the after school RFP because that was the biggest RFP that was going to be going through Passport.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: With all the glitches in the system, we didn't know if it was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so I do want to make sure that as much as I yell at folks, I like to make sure that I'm giving them their flowers.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: When things...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: actually happen and it works out.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so thank you for, you know, working through that and ensuring that it went out with no hiccups.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But just to kind of piggyback off of some of the stuff that the WIT was just talking about, Camilla Hanks,

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: especially in the human service sector, we know that they typically have a lot of issues and sometimes even when they're going through the process,

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: when it's lit up on the bubble, that's not where the contract is.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And it kind of gets difficult to figure out where you are in the process.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so my question is, so just to start off, like, what are you, what improvements are you doing to make Passport do what it should be doing?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because my pushback is always that, you know, we know that we need a system that is working and it's not about just blowing up Passport.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's about thinking about if this isn't working, then what are we doing to make it work?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But like specifically, I know one of the things that I've heard often is that like you

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They'll look into Passport and the space where it says that the contract is, it's not.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so even that function, sometimes it's difficult to find out where they're at in the process.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So what are some of the things that you guys are doing to improve that so that providers could use it in a functional way?

chapters.summary: Yu admits there are gaps and user-experience issues, says system stability, payment predictability, and contracting predictability are North Stars, and that Release 7 will be the focus while avoiding changes that compromise predictability.
chapters.title: Yu acknowledges PASSPort gaps and discusses stability and Release 7

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Vice Chair Stevens, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And thank you so much for recognizing that large, large procurement that we did on Compass.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It really was an all-hands effort in DYCD, the procuring agency.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: They really rolled up their sleeves, and we were happy to...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: support that because it meant after school for a lot of kids who did not previously have after school.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And that was a Herculean effort.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I gave them so many kudos, which I never do.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They've been amazing.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So yes.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Wanted to give you your kudos as well.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You played a part in that as well.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So to answer your question,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: There are gaps.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I'm going to be very upfront.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: There are gaps.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We have tried very hard through a technology solution to solve for many problems and answer to many people.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And as we evolve the project, it really is about taking a moment and seeing how far we've come, but then also seeing where is...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Where are we falling short to some of our providers, our nonprofit providers?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And what is that gap attributable to?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Is it the technology?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Is it change management?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Is it something else?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: You were not the first to lift up and raise that there are user experience issues.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It is a very common issue that is brought up.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And it's something that in this moment where we are with the project, system stability,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: along with payment predictability and contracting predictability, those are our North Stars.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And the system stability, you okay, Chair?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm good.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The flags are attacking you.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The system stability is very...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: critical.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I'm also not going to be shy about that there were times where the system experienced a little bit of turbulence because of the changes we were doing to the system in a very short amount of time.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And what we have observed, having the benefit of looking back, when we

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: change the system, sometimes we shake the system a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And that, our users experience it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Our nonprofits experience it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Our construction firms experience it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Our agencies experience it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So one of the things that we are trying to do is we're going to focus on Release 7.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Which I spoke about in the testimony, but we're also going to really try to be very thoughtful about not introducing new things into the system that maybe compromise payment predictability and contracting predictability.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But yes, there is work that we need to do to get in there and hear from the users what it is that they are experiencing and their needs are not being met.

chapters.summary: Stevens says providers fear telling funders about problems; Yu says MOCS reviews tickets, surveys vendors on functionality, and convenes industry groups to hear candid feedback.
chapters.title: Stevens asks how providers give feedback; Yu describes collection methods

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How are you?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Folks able to give you back that feedback?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What does that feedback process look like?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because again, it gets really hard.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And this is one of the things that I try to explain to the city.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's really hard for groups to be able to tell providers and people who are giving them money that they're messing up.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So what is the expectation and how is that supposed to, like how, How are you guys collecting that feedback?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because, you know, that is always a struggle for me.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because everyone's like, no, we're working with...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I'm like, you know the providers are telling me different stuff that they're telling you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because they can't tell you that because you're giving them money.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yes, it's a fair point.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: There are a few ways that I think we pick up the signs in addressing that maybe they're not as direct as raising a direct complaint.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We look at the tickets, so a vendor's experiencing an issue on the procurement system and also on Passport.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And we are reviewing the tickets, and are there patterns that we can discern from what we're getting?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The other thing we do is we do proactively try to survey our vendors on particular pieces of the Passport functionality.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Most recently, we did it for the vendor reports that we turned on earlier this year, and we're trying to see what we can glean from there.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And then also at certain moments we will convene particular industries or particular groups and we will ask them to tell us how we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And they are not shy about it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: They do not hold back.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I was supposed to ask some of Lincoln's questions, but I'll just leave that to him.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Thank you for the time.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks if the administration supports Intro 1064; Ochoa says the main delay is agreeing with contractors whether work is a change order, not the registration process, and he is open to a clock once a change order is agreed.
chapters.title: Wilson asks about Intro 1064 and change-order delays

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vice Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I will now kick it to Councilmember Wilson, followed by Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I just want to ask a couple questions about my two pieces of legislation, starting with 1064, which would require DDC to set timeframes for agency approvals and change order determinations.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Does the administration support entry of 1064?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I feel like there's a way to pass this bill that is beneficial to both what you're trying to get at and what the agency is trying to do.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And I'll tell you, I get really frustrated with change orders, but the main delay that we see in change orders is not the process itself of putting a change order together and sending it to the controller for registration.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It is agreeing with the contractor that something is a change order.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And this is what our project managers and engineers do.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Essentially what happens is the contractor may say, that's outside the contract change order because that's automatically where they would go to.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We then say, no, no, it is definitely within scope.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It's within the contract.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: You should do it, and there's no need for a change order.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And so that back and forth, which is very, very common, unfortunately, is what soaks up the most time.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And it's hard to put a clock on that.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I am happy to put a clock on when we agree to a change order.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Nothing should be delayed.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We usually take about a month internally to put a package together and then send it to the controller's office of registration.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: The controller then has a month.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So we're talking about a two-month period, which to me sounds pretty reasonable, but it's this back and forth where we spend the most time and I think where the frustration usually lies.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks whether agencies set internal deadlines for change orders; Ochoa says the city sets payment timelines but not change-order timelines, and DDC usually takes about two months once a change order is agreed, with back-and-forth sometimes lasting four or five months.
chapters.title: Wilson asks about internal deadlines and average DDC change-order time

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Do any agencies currently set internal deadlines for acting on change order requests other than request or other contract approvals?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Yeah, it's a really good question.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: You know, the last administration had a capital reform task force that was looking at it.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: a lot of these issues.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We're going to be restarting it soon, and we're happy to share that information when we're finalized.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: But it is something that we can look at.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I think we set, the city set times on payments, so invoicing timelines.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I don't believe we had an agreement on change order timelines, but I think it's worth a discussion for sure.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And on average, how long does DDC take to act on a change order request?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: On a project of this size?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: When we agree there's a change order, it's usually about a two-month period.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It's agreeing to the change order that I think takes the longest time.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And sometimes it can take, you know, four or five months of just back and forth.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I would say, though, most of these sentences, the work is continuing and a change order shouldn't stop the actual construction.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: There are times when we are discussing change orders for work that will happen nine months from now, just in anticipation of that.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So it is frustrating and we could do better, but it's also our job to make sure that the contractors are doing what they're supposed to be doing.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks if the administration supports cost benchmarks; Ochoa supports publishing backward-looking contract data but worries about forward-looking estimates because construction costs change, and says the city has data but not easily searchable.
chapters.title: Wilson asks about Intro 1065 cost benchmarks

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And then for 1065, which is the cost benchmarks.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Does the administration support that?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I am happy to do anything backwards looking.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So essentially our contracts are public, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And so whenever we put out a contract for a boiler replacement or a roof replacement, we can absolutely publish that.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I'm a little worried of...

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Putting what we think is the estimate of what a future project would look like, just because the economics of

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: of construction change very frequently.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And so, for example, right now, the construction costs are about 8% a year.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And that can change at any given time because of factors outside of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Data centers are soaking up a lot of the raw materials that we would normally use for construction, steel, concrete.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And so we've seen the prices of those materials increase, and it would be hard for me to put a benchmark there and then something like this happens and the numbers are outdated.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: But I think it's a good idea to have a sort of a list of items that we've paid for for all these small capital projects.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So I feel like there's a way to achieve what you're aiming to achieve and what we feel comfortable doing.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Does the city have data on the actual total costs of completed small capital projects, and which system does that data come from?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Yeah, we definitely have the data.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It is something that we look at, too, when we are estimating projects on our front-end planning.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I don't think it's easily available or searchable for somebody in the public, but all our contract data is available.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We just haven't packaged it together, I think, in the way that you would want it.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And would benchmarks under this bill be consistent with the benchmarks in the mayor's management report?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Yeah, the MMR has benchmarks not on

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: They have benchmarks on commitments as a whole.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So we essentially have capital commitments that we are aiming for on any given year.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We also have timelines, construction timelines that we include.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So if the goal is to unline it, I believe we can.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Right on time.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thanks so much, Councilmember Wilson, and thank you for the thoughtful legislation.

chapters.summary: Brewer says she came from a child care hearing where payment and insurance were major issues, and asks whether insurance plays into contracting discussions.

chapters.summary: Ochoa says DDC hears about insurance constantly and is working on a Contractor Controlled Insurance Program for borough-based jails and an owner-controlled insurance program to reduce barriers for smaller firms.
chapters.title: Ochoa describes DDC insurance programs CSIP and OSIP

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: Well, no, so I'm asking just two things, though, just so you know that's what was happening.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But also, on the insurance, which came up here and everywhere else, does that play into any discussion in terms of the contracting?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know it has something to do with you, per se, and it is a state issue, but it is constant.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: There's two programs that DDC is working on with the administration.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: There is a program called CSIP, which is the Contractor Controlled Insurance Program, that we're using for our entire borough-based jail program.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: That means that they can negotiate better prices.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: That means they're not having burdens of smaller firms trying to get insurance.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm just saying we all need to work on insurance.

utterances.text: the work to clear out, we're calling it clear the queue.

utterances.text: And we're asking the agencies to go in and everything that predates October 1st, 2026.

utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.text: We're asking them to identify what roadblock exists.

chapters.summary: Ochoa says PASSPort is not a construction project management system and that DDC front-end planning may increase project scope before funding is secured, so cost increases may not appear as overruns in PASSPort.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: No, that may have been the case.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I don't see Passport as a project management, as a construction project management system.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It is a procurement system.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But for tracking spend?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And so we're processing some of the payments through Passport, but not all the payments.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I think that if I misstated that, I don't mean it as a project management tool, but I think as a tool for effectively tracking our spend.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And when we're severely over budget, it's a way for us to know that and see that and be able to course correct or adjust accordingly.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: They give us a project.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: They say, and I'm making up the numbers.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I'm not picking up on the Parks Department.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: They think it's a $5 million project.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: When we go through front-end planning process and we look at everything, we say, well, yes, the roof is at the end of their useful life, but then there's also the A-track that sits on the roof that's nearing the end of useful life.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And so we're recommending that we do both.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So what started as a $5 million project may end up as an $8 million project.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: But that's not cost overrun.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: That is just a proper scoping of a project.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And so we won't take the project until the $8 million are funded.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And so by the time it gets to Passport, we already have the full funding.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And so the only thing you may be able to track are potential change orders on any given project, but not the cost increases, I think, in the way that people think about cost increases, because that happens in the front end to make sure that we are lining up with.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: one, actual construction costs, and two, proper scoping of projects.

utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You were relying on multiple systems to track things, which is just unacceptable, right, and has to change.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And if Passport isn't the solution, and Passport, I mean, is clunky, right, then understanding what is the solution I think is really important.

chapters.summary: Ochoa says DDC has separate project management, invoice, and timeline systems and is developing a technology roadmap to consolidate them into one user-friendly system for project managers, contractors, and eventually the public.
chapters.title: Ochoa discusses multiple DDC systems and technology roadmap

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Yeah, you know, one of the first things I've done and I did as commissioner was looking at all our technology systems.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: You are correct, council member, that we have a project management system.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We have an invoice system and we have a timeline system.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: There's no reason for that.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So we are looking.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We do have a really good technology roadmap.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: to update all those systems into one that makes sense and that's easily user-friendly for the project manager, but also for the contractor and eventually for the public if we want to do that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And if I was following you right a moment ago, I feel like I totally appreciate you have said to me several times over these six months, you know, that agency will anticipate the cost of something is X, and then when DDC actually looks under the hood, cost is X plus Y plus Z.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But what I'm– and I get that that's going to happen once, you know, the architects and engineers analyze something.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Costs are going to be different than whatever, you know, city agency might have anticipated.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But what I want to make sure of is that when we have an estimate on a project that we know the spend is happening, that we're staying within budget, I think–

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: What we really highlighted at that hearing six months ago is that I think too many vendors get away with submitting a bid at a lower price and then making adjustments along the way and submitting mods that don't end up being that lowest price.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we could have gone with a better vendor that has a better track record, and we get sucked into those bad decisions.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so we continue to want to see reforms in these areas.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I, you know, I maybe to.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Well, I'll give you a second if you want to respond.

chapters.summary: Ochoa says DDC is changing evaluation culture to ensure fair contractor evaluations and that alternative delivery allows best-value selection rather than lowest bid, which he argues is cheaper long-term.
chapters.title: Ochoa discusses contractor evaluations and best-value delivery

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, it drives me crazy too.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We have seen that sometimes the lowest bidder, we don't feel like they can do the job that they're bidding on.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So what we're doing is a couple things.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: The threshold for finding them not responsive or not responsible is pretty high.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Understandable.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: But what we're doing at DDC is changing the culture of evaluations to make sure they're writing fair and true evaluations of every single contractor.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Because the evaluations is actually what the city determines as a basis for potentially finding them not responsive or not responsible.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And I don't think historically the agency was taking that seriously.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So that's one piece.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: The other piece is alternative delivery doesn't bound us by the lowest bidder.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It is the best value.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And that does not, obviously prices are taken into account, but we also look at experience.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We also look at the type of quality that they've delivered and the teams that they're putting together.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: To me, best value ends up being cheaper on the long run than just following lowest bid contracting.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Those are reforms I think we should pursue together.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm happy to hear you reference a plan to kind of revisit the Capital Reform Project Task Force that Director Suleiman led with then-First Deputy Mayor Grillo some four years ago.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We hope the council will be a partner in that effort.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And look forward to more information and updates on that.

chapters.summary: Restler asks about Intro 991; Ochoa distinguishes standard designs from design guidelines, cites five Parks bathrooms at $3.6M each done twice as fast, and explains deep sewer and electrical infrastructure drives costs.
chapters.title: Restler asks about standard designs; Ochoa discusses design guidelines and park bathroom costs

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I have one more question for you, which is just relating to Councilmember Banks'legislation.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I understand that we need flexibility, that every project is different.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And at the same time, I would think that...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Standardization could improve timelines and reduce costs.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so, you know, I think that you were testifying against the bill today, although you were diplomatic and nice.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you just give a little more?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: To me, there's a difference between standard designs, which the bill is asking for, and design guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And I'm a huge fan of design guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
