utterances.text: And so, for example, we're doing five bathrooms for the Parks Department with very strict and clear design guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you want to tell us how much they each cost?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: $3.6 million.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Each?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: $3.6 million for a bathroom.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: They're going to be done in a total of about 18 months, two times faster than they would have done their traditional design bit built.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: But I do want to address that because it's not just a structure.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So, for example, we were at a casino park in Flushing yesterday, and the bathroom that we're building is in the middle of the park.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: There is no sewer connection.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: There's no electricity connection in the middle of the park.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So I know the price tag can sometimes be daunting if you're just looking at it at face value, but there's a lot of work that needs to happen for that building to be actually functional.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And from the park, from the bathroom that we're building to the public right-of-way, that's about half a mile of just deep sewer and electricity infrastructure that we have to build.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So those tend to drive up the cost significantly.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But how close is it to the velodrome?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It's actually very close.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay, good.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Yeah, it's right next to it.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It's beautiful.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Gennaro joins the conversation about the velodrome in Kissena Park, and Ochoa confirms DDC was there yesterday and that the park bathroom project is nearby.
chapters.title: Gennaro and Ochoa discuss Kissena Park velodrome

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Did you know about the velodrome in Kissimmee Park?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: It's cool.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It's very cool.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Queens, you know?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I know, I'm Brooklyn, but you should know about the Village Room.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It's cool.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It is very nice.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We were just there yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: You can see my video next week.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: You're really popping those out.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: How many videos a week are you doing now, Commissioner?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: The type of infrastructure that a new bathroom inside a park requires is pretty significant.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It's not something that the New Yorkers see, but I do think it's important for them to understand so that they know why the costs are so high.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you have one more question for Commissioner Ochoa?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks whether parks have capital plans so costs are known before projects happen, saying agencies and elected officials often have different expectations and elected officials get blamed.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about proactive capital planning for parks

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: When you talk about the infrastructure issues, is there a space where parks have those capital plans laid out so that we know what these costs are going to be before they happen?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It happens very often in school construction authority to where there's no real forethought and

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Sometimes agencies can become in their bubble, and our goals are very different.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We want to say, hey, we have the funding, we want to do X, Y, and Z.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And then you have your goals and what the funding actually looks like.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And there's a huge disparity between the two.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So is there anything that we can do to kind of do, which is not something that the city does, which is proactive work?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Just a little bit, because then we wouldn't be here, right?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so we're the borough of parks, and we have tons of parks.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: whatever, but it would be great if there would be some sort of anticipation that there are certain parks and spaces and capital projects that we know that we're going to have to do

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: that, yes, a chair costs a million dollars and no one understands, you know, and I see the guys who work for the city nodding their head, of course you have to.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But I think that there is a space where we must have some of the same language and some proactive work so we're not daunted because what ends up happening is that we will say this is what we want to do as elected officials.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We ask you, you come back with something, but we get blamed.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I don't want to get blamed anymore.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ochoa says DDC is launching advanced capital planning, sending inspectors to city-owned buildings for two-week assessments of needs over five to 10 years, to help agencies plan better and avoid cost surprises.
chapters.title: Ochoa describes advanced capital planning assessments

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And it's not just a parks issue.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It's a library issue where an elected official will give $2 million for what the, let's call it NYPL or BPL or QPL, thinks is a $2 million project.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We take it.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It turns out to be a $3.5 million project.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And then the library system will go back to you and say it's a $3.5 million project.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: But by the time you add the other 1.5, it's been one fiscal year.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And so then when they give us the 3.5, it's now actually 4.2.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So it's really, really frustrating.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: But we do have a pretty good solution in the works.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It's called advanced capital planning.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And what that means is we're going to be sending inspectors to all city-owned buildings and a couple of cultural institutions to do a full assessment.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Like aims on steroids, a full assessment of the building to see what they need and what they will need in the next five to 10 years so that the agencies can do better planning ahead of time.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And so we're going to go in and say the facade looks okay, but we think you're going to have to replace it in the next

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: five years.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: The boiler looks okay, but we think you're going to need to replace it in the next three years.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: What do you think it'll cost to do the assessment per building?

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: It's going to be about a two-week assessment per building.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Right now, it's about a three-hour assessment, and so it's a much deeper assessment of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: This was something that was...

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Partially funded a few plans ago that we're rolling, we're almost done with the application, and it's going to be great because then it'll allow sponsor agencies to be able to ask for money if they need it, but to just do better capital planning to make sure that doesn't happen.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Restler thanks Ochoa and dismisses him from the hearing, joking that he hopes this kindness is remembered.
chapters.title: Restler dismisses Commissioner Ochoa

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Well, I think that I'm going to do something that's unusually nice.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And dismiss Commissioner Ochoa.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I just hope this is remembered in the future.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I feel like I'm going to be back.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And you could stay all afternoon and not have to remember it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But, you know, I'm just kidding.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The last chance, council members, if you have anything for the commissioner.

chapters.summary: Brewer says libraries do not like DDC, Ochoa says DDC had a productive meeting with libraries and cultural institutions hosted by Councilmember Williams, and Restler thanks Ochoa and his team.
chapters.title: Brewer raises library-DDC tensions as Ochoa departs

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I just want to say, as great as you are, the libraries don't like you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: They don't like DDC.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's not that they dislike Paul particularly, right?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yeah, but he's in charge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: He's in charge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I like you, and I like the libraries, but you all don't get along.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: We had a large meeting yesterday with Councilmember Williams that she hosted with the cultural institutions and the libraries, all systems.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I think we've made a ton of progress over the last six months.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: I think we're doing much better.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: And a lot of it was just communication and making sure that they understand our expectations, their expectations, and then involving them in the process.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: So I think we're doing much better.

utterances.speaker: Paul Ochoa
utterances.text: You should check with Iris to see what she says.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Always listen to Iris.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Commissioner and team.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I just want to say we appreciate your reference to AIMS on steroids.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We look forward to advancing our AIMS legislation.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Hopefully, OMB will be as cooperative as DDC is in that endeavor.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Nice to see you, Director.

chapters.summary: Restler says the city has spent about $120M on PASSPort, including $97M with iValua and $20M+ with Accenture; Yu says the project price tag is $151.4M, with iValua licensing about $2.5M per year and Accenture systems integration about $7.5M per year.
chapters.title: Restler asks about PASSPort costs and vendor contracts

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We will now dig into Passport Fund.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Our review found that the city has spent about $120 million on Passport since

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: its inception and kind of design back in 2016, including $97 million with Invalua on creation and updates and $20 million plus with Accenture.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you just give us a kind of very quick overview of the costs and the services that are provided under the I Value a Contract and the Accenture contract?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Chair, I'd be happy to.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So our number is actually a little higher.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The number that we like to, the price tag we put on the passport project so far is $151.4 million.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And the other price tag that's readily handy is the Release 7 work, which is $6.5 million.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But just to, again, take a step back.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I'll go into the weeds a little bit, so please indulge me.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So two contractors, two contracts.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We've got iValua.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: IValua is the software provider.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The city of New York licenses the software from iValua, and we pay around $2.5 million per year for that license.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We also have a relationship with Accenture.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Accenture is what we call, for just shorthand, our systems integrator.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And we pay about $7.5 million per year.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So Passport as a system per year as a baseline is $10 million.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: That's just steady state.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The cost will go up or you will see costs go up year to year if there are changes to the functionality, which we call releases, or there are upgrades to the system.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So that is when you will see peaks of increased.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: funding over the life of the contracts and over the life of the project.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Restler asks about renewal timelines; Yu says current contracts expire April 2027, there is no renewal option, and MOCS may pursue a negotiated acquisition after an earlier solicitation did not proceed.
chapters.title: Restler asks about PASSPort contract renewals

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So just so I– those contracts, are they– what is the renewal timeline on those contracts?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The current contracts are set to expire April 2027.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And then you have a renewal option on them?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We do not.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So does that mean you'd have to...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Put out a new solicitation at that point?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Or what are your options?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We could, and we did earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We did not see that through.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Most likely we will do what we call a negotiated acquisition.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Did they kind of, did both of them, well,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay, fair enough.

chapters.summary: Restler asks about staffing; Yu says it is hard to parse because procurement operations liaisons support agencies and PASSPort, estimates roughly 30-40 people on the service desk and technology side, and notes MOCS has 170 staff.
chapters.title: Restler asks how many MOCS staff focus on PASSPort

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How many staff positions at MOX are focused on Passport?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: You know, it's an interesting question when we try to parse out how much of our PS budget goes to the Passport project.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And I wanted to go back to just sort of your prior question just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: This extends beyond just the passport project.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: This extends to all vendors who have a relationship with the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I value and Accenture are our partners in providing this citywide enterprise system, and they've been our partners for 10 plus years now.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And we have had some ups and downs in our relationship with our vendors, and I hope that going forward in our negotiations,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: we are a valued partner to them just as we are entering into those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But on your question around how many of our team members support Passport, it's hard to really parse out because, and I'll give you a little bit of an anecdote or example.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We have a team called our Procurement Operations Team.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Our Procurement Operations Team maintains a relationship with our city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And, for example, Commissioner Ochoa was here.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: At MOX, there is a MOX Procurement Operations Team member assigned to DDC.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And so as DDC is moving its procurements, contracts, and payments through Passport, they will work with their MOX procurement operations liaison.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So that person is over helping them project plan their procurements, helping them, advising them which procurement method is best.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And then from time to time, if there are passport issues, they will help on passport.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So is that person designated to the passport project?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's hard to say.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: A portion of their time is designated to it, but it's not a clean one-to-one that person is assigned to the passport project.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you have any way of kind of thinking about a full-time employee equivalence or anything that could give us some sense of scale?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Or do you have a way of how you, if, I mean, like, how would, yeah, how would you think about it if?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We could certainly parse it out.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm not, or maybe a less exact answer.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you give us like a ballpark sense?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Ballpark?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Let's see.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I would want to give you a precise response, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I really would.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So if I could, I'd take this one back.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Or maybe a different question would be, like, how many folks are just on the technical side of managing the iValua and Accenture contracts that just, like, you have on a team there?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: On our technology team,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's interesting because we also have what we call our mock service desk team.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And our mock service desk team owns the relationship with our vendors.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And so they are helping our vendors move through city contracting and procurement.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And a part of their responsibility is passport.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And so roughly maybe 30 to 40 people.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But again, I would really want to come back to you on that number.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Right, because your headcount total is a few hundred?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Less than it should be.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But we should talk.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So it's a significant portion of your headcount is focused on this, and a significant portion of MOX operations are dedicated to this technology management.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: roughly, roughly could be as high as 20 or 30%, even higher potentially.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So that's a lot.

chapters.summary: Restler asks whether OTI is involved day-to-day; Yu says OTI's involvement has ebbed and flowed, MOCS is the business owner, and OTI has recently been engaged on strategic questions about PASSPort's future.
chapters.title: Restler asks about OTI involvement in PASSPort

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you just articulate, is OTI involved in managing Passport?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Are they directly engaged in the day-to-day here?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for the question.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We are, you know, OTI's involvement in the Passport Project has ebbed and flowed.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Initially, at the inception of the project, it was an OTI project.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Through the passage of time, there have been handoffs from OTI to MOX.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: MOX will always be the business owner of this project.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We are the procurement subject matter experts.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: More recently, we have asked OTI to come in to have some more strategic conversations about passports, some of which you mentioned at the top, Chair, around what is the future of passport, what is the future of e-procurement,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: how do we improve the user experience.

chapters.summary: Restler says OTI is usually central to city technology infrastructure and asks if more OTI involvement could free MOCS capacity; Yu says she would welcome it for the large project.
chapters.title: Restler asks if OTI should be more involved; Yu welcomes it

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So more recently, we were having conversations with OTI and that team on those bigger, larger questions, not on the day-to-day, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Should they be more involved?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I mean, I think generally OTI is pretty directly involved in most technology management, management of most critical technology infrastructure for the city.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm a little surprised that they're less involved here.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you think they could be an asset?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you think it could free up MOX capacity, potentially do?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Other important work if OTI was more involved?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I would welcome it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I would welcome it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's a big project.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's a big undertaking.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And having those who have something to contribute and offer is welcomed.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I mean, it's just, it's worth remembering.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: a system that moves tens of billions of dollars annually, has tens of thousands of users and hundreds of thousands of transactions, right?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I mean, like, it's a big, complex technology endeavor.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You would think that our technology agency would be centrally engaged in it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So maybe that's a future thing for us to raise with Councilmember De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And our friends over at OTI, which is based in District 33, just noting.

chapters.summary: Restler asks about capital eligibility of PASSPort improvements; Yu says the city licenses rather than owns the software, making it a non-starter under controller directives, and that any change would likely be forward-looking.
chapters.title: Restler asks why PASSPort improvements are not capital eligible

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Adoption of passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So, oh, I do want to just want to dig a little further here.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: One other thing that has been a bugaboo of mine is capital eligibility of passport improvements.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you just help us understand why the kind of updated releases and improvements to Passport are not capably eligible?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I guess relatedly, is there any mechanism that we could take over this system and have it be city-owned?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Councilmember, thank you for raising this.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: This is something that also frustrates our MOX finance team.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The way that the passport project is structured and the way the contracts are set up, as I mentioned, we are licensing a software.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So essentially we rent.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We do not own.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And so for capital eligibility, that makes it a non-starter under the controller directives.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I think my, I know this very, very generally, not deeply.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: My understanding is the controller has revisited the capital eligibility on software.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I do not believe.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: This controller?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: This controller.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: No, don't hold me to that.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Okay, might have been the last one.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: May have been the last one.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I will say that I don't believe it will ever be backwards looking.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It will likely be forwards looking around capital eligibility.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Restler asks if there is any way to make the system city-owned; Yu describes a conceptual option to purchase iValua's intellectual property or build a city-owned e-procurement system, and Restler offers to engage the comptroller, law, and OMB.
chapters.title: Restler and Yu discuss city ownership options for PASSPort

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So you don't think there's any way to get it to shoehorn it in?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: There is one idea, and this is a very conceptual idea, and it would take a lot of folks to buy in.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We could purchase the intellectual property.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: iValue provides an off-the-shelf solution.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We have customized and configured the solution to serve the specificity of the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: All of that work.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Is owned by Evalua.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And are they a willing seller?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Are we a willing buyer?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We are very, that is just one of the myriad of options.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Now, if we were to sort of blue sky or whiteboard, you could have our e-procurement system that is owned by the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Which is

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: City of New York technologists, City of New York coders, they build a system.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And we would, but that is something that is far out.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's a new system.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: That would be a replacement system.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's if we're moving on.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Look, that's all interesting and helpful.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If there are any conversations for us to try to have with the controllers team, we'd be happy to participate in them and try to help push, as well as with law and OMB.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I think that I imagine...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, there's an interplay between some of the ideas that you just laid out and the expiration of a contract.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so we're thinking about all these things together and appreciate you laying out some of the moving parts that you're considering.

chapters.summary: Restler asks about stages or contracts outside PASSPort; Yu says all mayoral agencies are in, but non-mayoral agencies like DOE and School Construction Authority are not.
chapters.title: Restler asks what procurement still happens outside PASSPort

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just, you know, it's been, it was a gradual kind of rollout of Passport, I think delayed by COVID.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: HHS Accelerator finally kind of incorporated back in 2024, just a couple of years.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: HHS Accelerator, I should say, was finally decommissioned just a couple of years ago, back in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Are there any stages of the procurement process or certain contracts that are processed outside of Passport at this point?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Anyone we should beat up?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: There are bits and pieces, but certainly all the mayoral agencies are in.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The non-mayoral agencies are not in.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Organizations such as the Department of Education, school construction.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Among the mayoral agencies.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Right, among the mayoral agencies.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: There are some folks who maybe are out, but for the most part, everybody is in.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So there's nothing that comes to mind that you would highlight or flag for us of folks that are continuing to operate outside of the system?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Among mayoral agencies.

chapters.summary: Restler cites a 2022 nonprofit task force on legacy systems; Yu says she is not aware of legacy systems still in use among mayoral agencies, though some underground processes may exist.
chapters.title: Restler asks about legacy systems forcing duplicate information

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Are there any, the 2022 nonprofit task force of kind of getting, I think it was like getting nonprofits paid or something like that,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: reference other old contract legacy systems at certain agencies, forcing users to enter duplicative information.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Are there any of these legacy systems still in use to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Among the mayoral agencies?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: That's not to say that it doesn't exist and it might be underground.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But for the most part, you know, we have done a lot of work to make sure that everybody's in.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Cool.

chapters.summary: Restler asks about budget adjustments and contract amendments handled by email outside PASSPort; Yu says it is hard to quantify offline activity but the goal is one source of truth in PASSPort.
chapters.title: Restler asks how much contracting still happens by email

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How much is still happening via email and not captured in Passport?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For example, we've heard the need to adjust budgets because of indirect costs and COLAs and contracts that need to be amended because of new needs that are handled entirely by email and that Passport would not actually reflect those issues.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is that a common practice?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: That's hard to quantify, I would say.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's hard to quantify.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The idea is that if you have everything in one system and there's one source of truth, it provides the visibility and it provides all the advantages of everything being in one place.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I'm sure that there are some offline processes that are happening as a result of just...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: You know, ease, necessity, it's hard for me to quantify that offline activity.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And this is something we've heard from the controllers team over the past year.

chapters.summary: Restler asks about the interface between PIP and PASSPort; Yu says Release 6 decommissioned part of PIP and moved subcontracting functionality into PASSPort, but PIP still exists and full integration is not on the horizon.
chapters.title: Restler asks about PIP and PASSPort integration

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you help explain to me the interface between PIP and Passport?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And have there been conversations to more kind of closely link these systems or integrate these systems or having the controller be a user of Passport?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is any of that stuff on the table right now?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Certainly there have been prior conversations around...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The relationship of PIP and passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And you worked in the controller's office.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So you have seen both sides.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So most recently with release six, which happened 2024, I believe, a portion of PIP was decommissioned and a piece of functionality was stood up in Passport.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And this is around the subcontracting.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: PIP still exists, however.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: PIP exists.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's jointly owned by the mayoralty and the controller, and it involves city vendors needing to disclose information so that they can effectively be paid electronically.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Those are some, that would be,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: That would be quite the lift if we were to ever completely subsume PIP into Passport.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But so those conversations are not on the horizon.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Better linking or integrating the systems?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is that something that we should be thinking about?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Because did the systems talk effectively to one another today?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: That I would have to take back.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And certainly, I would have to take that one back.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Restler notes MOCS once said Release 2 would be final and asks about Release 7; Yu says pending budget modifications currently block invoice submission, citing 10,000 budget mods last fiscal year, and Release 7 will remove that stop.
chapters.title: Restler asks about Release 7 functions

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Release 7.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think Mox testified back in 2019 when Justin Brannan chaired the Contracts Committee that Release 2 would be the final major release on Passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Throwback.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Wow.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You can thank Alex.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: He was here and asked Alex to and asked Justin to ask the question back then.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Seven years later, we're on Release 7.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you explain, I know you did in your testimony, but just once again succinctly, the functions that will be added through Release 7?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And in particular, nonprofits will now be able to submit invoices while budget mods and budget approvals are still pending.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Councilmember, you essentially said it in that last part.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And I can, to add, I can give you a sense of scale.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So last fiscal year, we count 10,000 budget modifications.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So during the pendency of those 10,000 budget modifications, which...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: On average, maybe we're in the system for five days.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So 10,000 times for those five days, there was an inability to submit an invoice into the passport for review for payment.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But fast forward, we hope for everybody to have

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: a smooth delivery of Release 7, that will no longer be a stop.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Pending budget modification will not stop invoice submission.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: Restler says the budget-mod and invoice block is the number one PASSPort complaint and confirms with Yu that Release 7 remains on track for early 2027.
chapters.title: Restler confirms Release 7 timing and notes top complaint

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I will say I think this is probably the number one complaint we've heard about Passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so it's really great that that's being fixed.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's not the only complaint we hear about Passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But I know that my vice chair and my colleague do often get a lot of Passport complaints.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I'd be interested if they have other items on their list of needed Passport changes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that, and just to confirm, you continue to be on track for an early 2027 release?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: Restler asks whether MOCS keeps a running list of requested reforms; Yu says yes, it is very long, and MOCS cannot do all of it.
chapters.title: Restler asks about PASSPort reform wish list

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you keep a running list of kind of reforms, requests of reforms or improvements, modifications that agencies, nonprofits, your own staff have identified?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Kind of like a wish list of changes to Passport?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's very long.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We cannot do all of it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Please don't ask us to do all of it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: No, it's good to know it exists because, I mean, look, as far as I understand it, and the vice chair can clarify, but I think the council really pushed.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For paying for these, really seven changes, and we continue to want to be a strong partner in advocating for updates if this is the system we're using.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Have you done a cost analysis of the changes on this list?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is there any more you can share?

chapters.summary: Yu says after Release 7 MOCS will pause to consider whether to keep building, stay the course, or remove functionality; she also mentions technology needs for the grant pilot and potential COGE initiatives.
chapters.title: Yu discusses post-Release 7 options and addition by subtraction

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So, Chair, in...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Thinking about this and what is the right approach about this going forward, there is an instinct to say that,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Let's change the system to make it better.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But there's also, there are other options.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And let's not change the system.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And maybe let's think about maybe we could take something out of this system to deprecate pieces of the system to make the experience better.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I'm not saying that that's where we are, but we are in a, after R7, when we catch our breath, we are going to take a moment and pause and think through what does make sense.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Does it make sense to continue to build?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Does it make sense to stay the course?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Does it make sense to maybe take out pieces of functionality and have them?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Those are the types of conversations that we'll be having soon.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Our seven is our priority, but sometimes it is underappreciated.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: What's the saying?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Addition by subtraction.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So we're open to exploring that as a potential path forward also.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Any short list of potential modifications that

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: additions by subtraction or just updates that you might share that you think are some of the priority things to consider post-release 7?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So, Council Member, one of the things that will...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We will have to confront is what is the technology solution for the grant pilot?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: What are the technology solutions for the COGE initiatives should they pass election day?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Those are things that we have to grapple with, that we have to do, versus what we want to do.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So those are things that would love to come to you in partnership and think through how we solution that through the technology.

chapters.summary: Restler thanks his chief of staff Molly and describes a medium-sized nonprofit that takes half a day to submit one invoice; he asks Yu whether that shocks her.
chapters.title: Restler raises nonprofit invoice submission burden

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that, you know, we'd love to join you to have some conversations with stakeholders of like, what are they thinking and create an opportunity for some,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: you know, constructive feedback as you kind of move beyond Release 7.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So maybe for next year.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I was struck, my chief of staff, Molly, and I, I didn't recognize Molly.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I didn't recognize you in my opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I forgot to do that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I want to just take a moment to thank Molly, who's the best, belatedly.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But Molly is the brains of our operation, and I'm grateful all the time for the opportunity to work with her.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Molly and I had a chance to sit down with a local nonprofit in our district earlier this week.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And they're a medium-sized nonprofit.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: They have lots of city contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: They're very competent.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And they told us it takes their staff member half a day to submit an invoice in Passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I don't know if that's similar to the kinds of things that you both hear from nonprofits in your communities.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But does that shock you?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Should it?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I don't, you know, like, how do you respond to that?

chapters.summary: Yu says it should not take that long and cites possible system issues, training gaps, and lost muscle memory; Restler describes Excel spreadsheets, no bulk upload, duplicate contract entries, and dozens of fields.
chapters.title: Yu responds to invoice burden; Restler details bulk-upload problems

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It should not be the case, and I have heard it before, and it goes to what I spoke of earlier, that we do know that there's some room for improvement and there's some gaps.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And anecdotally,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I think there could be a spectrum of reasons why it is taking that amount of time.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It could be that there could be a system issue.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: There could be a system issue.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It also could be we've got to do a better job.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Training the users.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It could be that there is, there are team members who are in the system

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: for periods of time and once you're in the system for a period of time you sort of know where to go, how to navigate, and then once you step away from the system and you haven't been in the system for a bit, a little bit of that muscle memory has been lost.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But yes, I have heard other providers share that things that their expectation of how long certain tasks take in Passport is beyond what

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: it's longer than they hope for.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Just to share, you know, when we sat with them, you know, they explained to us and showed us.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: They have all the information neatly organized in an Excel spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There's no mechanism for a bulk upload of an Excel file or kind of recognition of prior information, so they have to find the right contract amid seven kind of nearly identical entries

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: in the same contract to create a new invoice, upload the budget again, even though it hasn't changed, then go through each line item, entering the same service dates in every one of them, entering the invoice amount, the unit, the quantity price, dozens of fields that have to be transcribed from existing

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: documents into the right boxes, all in Passport, and each contract is different.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Agencies flip what info goes where, and it's just easy to make errors as a result.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so it just, it was surprising to me how unfriendly a user experience it was and how hard it was.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it's like, you know, these are,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: nonprofits that are spread thin and trying to do their best.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it just, I, I was like really empathetic to just the challenge that that staff are dealing with to get these, this information submitted and submitted correctly.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I, you know, I think that, um, I know that, you know, Mons is here to offer technical assistance and you guys have a help desk to try and help people through this stuff.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Um, but,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It just struck me that this is a lot harder than it should be.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So, please.

chapters.summary: Brewer says she receives many emails from groups that do not know if submissions are complete or whether problems are user error or technical glitches, and worries some groups will avoid city contracts.
chapters.title: Brewer adds concerns about opaque PASSPort submissions

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I just want to add to that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I didn't want to go through because I know this is a topic that Chair would.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: brought up, but it's just tons of emails to that effect.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I don't know how to address it, but it doesn't help people who want to work with the city.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I have a horrible feeling some groups say, I don't want to work with the city, I'll just stay in a private.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And they could be some of the best programs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I don't know how to, like I said, I don't know how to do it, but they don't know whether their submissions are complete.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That seems to be a big issue, as an example of something specific.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And they don't know whether it's user error or technical glitches.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's very opaque.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So, and I don't know whether you have, do you have like a 24 hour?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I assume some people do this off hours.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We do have some off hours.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: You have some off hours.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, that's great.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But all of that is still not addressing this problem.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So thank you.

chapters.summary: Restler asks how PASSPort handles frequent documents like budget docs and insurance forms, noting agencies require different forms for each contract; Yu says there is a need to standardize document requirements.
chapters.title: Restler asks about document vault and repeated insurance forms

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Brewer, as always, for just kind of having her finger on the pulse of the issues.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How is the system supposed to work for frequent documents like budget docs or insurance forms?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think we had, if I recall correctly, I don't remember, but I think Council Member Wan created the legislation on the document vault.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it sounded really good to me.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It doesn't sound like it's working as maybe envisioned.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you speak a little bit to like...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: to that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We hear from different, from like vendor, from nonprofits of like, we have to submit different insurance forms with different agencies for every single contract because

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: every agency wants the name of their agency on the contract, not just the city of New York, and that we have to resubmit the same documents all the time, and it's just frustrating.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And as explained, it's just kind of a slow process.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is there, I guess the question I'm trying to ask is like, is how, how are, how are, like how, or should things work with documents that need to be submitted time and again?

chapters.summary: Yu says the document vault is meant to work like a Google Drive but has had issues; MOCS completed a necessary upgrade over Indigenous Peoples' Day weekend, and she calls a quiet upgrade a good upgrade.
chapters.title: Yu describes document vault issues and recent upgrade

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Chair, I think there are two issues.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: There is the variability of.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Around what agency to agency is expecting from the providers.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And from the provider's perspective, it likely can seem a little bit like whiplash or getting bounced back and forth when they're

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: potentially providing the same services or the same insurance coverage documentation.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So there's that issue, which...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yes, there is a need to standardize to the extent that we can the document requirements that the city agencies are putting on our providers.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The other thing around the technology on the document vault itself, and I like to explain document vault is like a Google Drive.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's supposed to be a vault.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's supposed to be somewhere where you upload your documents and you're able to readily retrieve it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And I do know that there have been

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: There have been issues.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Throughout the time that we have introduced Document Vault into Passport.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I will say that we, over the Indigenous Day weekend, we did do a necessary upgrade to the Document Vault that Councilmember Wan legislated around.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: That was a necessary upgrade.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We were a little bit behind on doing that, but we are on the other side of that, and it was a successful upgrade.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I've learned in overseeing this technology project, even though I'm not a technologist, that a quiet upgrade is actually a good upgrade.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We don't want to hear about an upgrade.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So we are on the other side of that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's helpful.

chapters.summary: Restler asks how MOCS prioritizes urgent help desk requests; Yu says leadership triages work and gives examples.
chapters.title: Restler asks about help desk prioritization

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The help desk.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that you testified today to a reduction in average response times on the help desk, significant reduction, which is great.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you just elaborate a little about prioritization for urgent requests and kind of how you do that?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yeah, just speak to that a little more.

chapters.summary: Yu says MOCS prioritized PASSPort document-upload issues for the discretionary grant pilot and prioritizes bidder issues when a DDC bid is about to close.
chapters.title: Yu explains help desk prioritization examples

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We're talking a lot about technology today, but really when it comes down to it, we rely on our people to do this.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We rely on our people to identify the priorities and actually prioritize the work.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We have a really great leadership team overseeing the service desk.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: She leads this organization, and one of the things that will help prioritize how the work gets triaged and what gets worked on first, for example, Councilmember Brewer, you mentioned there's some

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: anxiety at the City Council around the discretionary grant process and whether or not

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: all of the agreements are going to get in to the pilot as we're hoping for.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I'm going to be very transparent about it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: There was an issue with Passport around uploading some documents to the pre-qualified list.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And because we know that the discretionary grant pilot is a strategic project of ours, all of the work, all of the

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: technology issues that we were observing in Passport, resolution of those issues was prioritized because we know we are in a short window to get this right.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The other example I can share about how we prioritize the service desk work, I'll pick on Commissioner Choa again because

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: He was here.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: DDC, let's say, has a bid that is set to close tomorrow on Friday.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Because we know that those who are interested in competing for that opportunity are in the system and there is a time sensitivity around getting their bids in, we will prioritize

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: the issues that those who are interested in competing for DDC's bid.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So those are some examples in how we prioritize the work.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's helpful.

chapters.summary: Restler says the Law Department's contracts division wants simultaneous OMB and law review in PASSPort and asks if it is on MOCS's radar; Yu says it is identified, tagged, and open to conversation.
chapters.title: Restler asks about simultaneous OMB and law review in PASSPort

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We've heard a healthy amount of feedback from agencies on changes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: They want to see the passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm sure you're keeping that list.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm sure their input is on your list.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: My favorite division in the law department, I'm not sure if I'm supposed to have favorites, but is the contracts and real estate division.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: They're my favorite, too.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: They're great.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just, so many smart people over the years that I admire so much, like Steve Stein Cushman and Howard Friedman and Amrita, like just very impressive group of folks.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: No disrespect to the other divisions in the law department, but, you know, we all have favorites.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Something we've heard from them is that they...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Would love to have simultaneous OMB and law review in Passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is this something that is on your radar?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you think it's something that we could consider incorporating into a future release?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How could we make our friends in the contracts division at the law department happy?

chapters.summary: Restler asks for a ballpark cost to add simultaneous OMB and law review; Yu says MOCS has not estimated it but will take the request back.
chapters.title: Yu says no cost estimate yet for law review change

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's something that is on our radar.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's something that law has a particular set of things that they would like to see in Passport.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We have identified it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We've tagged it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We've cataloged it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yes, I'm open to having those conversations.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you have any sense of a– I'm sure there are other reforms they would want to see as well, but any– is it possible to even provide a ballpark sense of cost for us to try to make a change like that?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I do not believe we've estimated the cost, but I will take that back.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Cool.

chapters.summary: Restler notes FY26 median invoice payment was 14 days versus six days in HHS Accelerator in 2019 and asks whether the cause is platform or agency users; Yu says city contracting scale grew and agency staffing has not kept up.
chapters.title: Restler asks about invoice processing times

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Some questions just on metrics and performance.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In FY26, the citywide, in the FY26 citywide indicators report showed that the median invoice processing payment was 14 days.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In 2019, the invoice payment timeline in the accelerator, in HHS accelerator, was reportedly six days.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Any ability to identify is this more of a platform issue or an agency user issue?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Any ability to kind of help diagnose the cause of those delays if the data points I'm using are, if I'm comparing apples to apples?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Sure, I'd have to take a deeper look.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yeah, you don't have the 2019 HHS accelerator data tattooed into your brain.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's fair.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But if it is accurate, any guess for why we might be looking at that?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Or is 14 days as a median invoice payment, is that kind of...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: A reasonable timeframe?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: At a very high level, I'll say that the scale of city contracting and nonprofit contracting in particular has grown exponentially over the COVID years.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: That could, and this touches upon a piece of legislation that you've introduced, the procurement and also agency

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Staffing capacity has not kept up.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Open question.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Something worthwhile for us to look at.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Fair.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's why we introduced it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I think we are looking forward to having a hearing on it.

chapters.summary: Restler asks for FY26 data on contracts registered after their start date; Yu says on-time registration was about 69% citywide and offers to follow up in writing.
chapters.title: Restler asks about contracts registered after start date

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Share of contracts registered in FY26 that were registered after their start date.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you know that data point?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We have the FY25 data.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Just wondering if you have updated.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We do have the FY26 indicators.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I want to say that we have some room to improve.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I think, I believe, just off memory, on-time registration was 69% citywide.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: On time with September 10th.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Because I thought what I was looking at for FY25 was that 72% were registered after the start date.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But we can dig in.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If it's something we could follow up on in writing, I think that would be helpful to just have the FY26 indicators and how we're comparing to previous years.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Restler notes median competitive sealed proposal time rose from 386 days in FY25 to 527 days in FY26 and asks if the old explanation that only payment timing matters still holds; Yu says context and predictability matter and the justification still resonates.
chapters.title: Restler asks about competitive sealed proposal timelines

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I wanted to ask about the median cycle time for competitive sealed proposals.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I did look back since Alex was highlighting 2019 City Council Contracts Committee hearings.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We did look back to what Dan Simon said then when this question was asked, and he basically said,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: that the number of days doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There are RFPs for bids, so they could start the RFP process two years before the contract is going to begin, or nine months, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And what actually matters is if someone's getting paid on July 1st when the contract starts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That was his argument.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You should tell me if that's the same argument that you would make.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But the...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The data on kind of the timeline for the competitive sealed proposals rose from 386 days in FY25 to 527 days in FY26.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: To be fair, the median length of time for competitive sealed bids declined year over year.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But just wondering any further, is Dan's explanation of this the right explanation?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you think this is an irrelevant data point that we shouldn't worry about and that what matters is when people are getting paid, not...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: how many years an agency plans preparing for an RFP?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I think multiple things can be true at once, and I think the context will matter.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And I do understand Dan's point.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Because it's really about predictability.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And if the provider is expecting July 1st, let's say 2027, to have a contract in place,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: and it's in place, I'm not sure how impactful it is that the agency and their planning activities initiated it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Maybe 18 months ago.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So from that perspective, that justification does continue to resonate.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that's fair.

chapters.summary: Restler says PASSPort's reporting is clunky and asks how it works and whether agencies have access; Yu says the data is vast, reporting requires discipline, and MOCS produces reports and uses Passport Public.
chapters.title: Restler asks about PASSPort reporting capabilities

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I do want to drill down on something that we've discussed a bit over the course of the year, which is just Passport as a management tool.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I think one of the greatest, one of the kind of most promising elements of Passport

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: from a decade ago was that it would serve as this management tool that would help us improve cycle times and identify and track specific issues that are causing delays.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It seems to me like the reporting capabilities of Passport are just very clunky and hard to...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: for us to benefit from.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you explain, like, could you walk us through the reporting capabilities of Passport, if that isn't too broad a question, and then kind of the agencies have access to those functions, or is that just a MOX, you know,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: is that just MOX's purview?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So on the reporting front,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The amount of data that is in the system is vast.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And with so much activity happening in the system, being able to extract what you need

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: and have a report to either tell you a compelling story or provide operational support, there is a whole discipline around reporting and developing reporting

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: and what you want to do with those reports.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Are they to provide insight?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Are they to prompt action?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And so that practice is one that requires a lot.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: There is a lot of reporting capability in Passport.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: There are a lot of things that MOX itself has pulled out of Passport, and we've prepared our own reports.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We've also asked, you know, I value an Accenture to make some reports readily accessible in Passport.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So it's a, there's a lot to unpack there.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But I think from the council's perspective, one of the things that I would lift up, we do have Passport Public.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Which is a database that is open to the public.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We also have, you know, for those who are interested, I'll lift up the Comptroller's Office checkbook database that provides a lot of information.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And for the agencies themselves, we do work with them to develop

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: reporting tools that will move their work that are appropriate for the agency's work, not appropriate for public consumption.

chapters.summary: Restler recalls DCAS waited months for a master-contract spending report; Yu says ad hoc requests can queue behind required reports, and the DCAS report revealed useful patterns.
chapters.title: Restler asks about DCAS master contract report

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I recall from conversations with Roman and the leadership team at DCAS that they had worked with you all to pull some reports on spending on master contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And my recollection was that it took a few months to pull it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you help us understand?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And my recollection from them at the time of the conversation was that they had not been able to get a report like this previously.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I imagine it was a relatively heavy lift on your all's part.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It took months, a bunch of staff time, not an easy thing to do.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: important.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
