utterances.text: Could you just, I guess you've spoken to this a little, but could you elaborate a little further on like why it's so hard to get these reports out of Passport?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And did, do you know if the data that was ultimately provided to DCAS was helpful in kind of understanding master contract spend and

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: there were insights that have helped shape better policy as a result?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I am familiar with that particular DCAS request for a report and information pulled from Passport.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I'll have to, just again based on memory, so big picture, MOX is responsible for lots of required reporting.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: From a variety of sources, council required reporting is a batch of them.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We also, we produce a lot of reports on not just procurement, but on spending and also on MWBE utilization.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So we do prioritize our legally required reports that we have to do.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: For ad hoc requests, sometimes they fall into a queue.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And that may have, I'm not saying for sure, but just generally speaking, sometimes that attributes to the delay on how fast we can turn around a report.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: On the DCAS report, I do remember seeing that particular report and

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: What is...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: What is beneficial for reports in that particular instance and in others is when you can see patterns emerge from the data.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And because there was enough information in that particular report, that pattern was very informative, but the pattern is also informative to

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: maybe be predictive in how we move forward.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So that one, that's my memory on that one without going too deeply into that one.

chapters.summary: Restler asks if PASSPort allows real-time tracking of contract registrations, budget mod approvals, and invoice payments; Yu says in part, the data is there, but MOCS relies on supplemental tools like Power BI.
chapters.title: Restler asks about real-time tracking of key metrics

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is there, does Passport allow for kind of real-time tracking of

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: key metrics that are priority, kind of priorities for you, like contract registrations, budget modification approvals, invoice payments?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Like, does Passport serve as an effective tool for you to be able to run reports and get good answers on, like, how efficiently you're doing?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: you're processing these things and getting this work done?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: In part, in part.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Certainly the information is there, the data is there.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We do rely on some supplemental tools to help us do what you're describing.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Also, there are

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: You know, one that's very common is there's a tool, Power BI.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Power BI is a very well-known tool for taking a lot of data and visualizing a certain way that's very easy to consume.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So from time to time, we do Power BI reports.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Restler asks whether iValua and Accenture contracts have performance metrics and how MOCS evaluates system functionality; Yu says MOCS tracks uptime, which was 99.1% or higher.
chapters.title: Restler asks how MOCS evaluates PASSPort performance

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm just going to do a few more topics and then we can call it a day.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm just interested in how you evaluate Passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Especially as you think about kind of looking ahead to a contract deadline, are there,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: ways did the Evalua and Accenture contracts have performance metrics connected to them or a performance component?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Are there metrics for Passport as a whole that you evaluate the system's functionality on?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's a great question that is worth continuing to evolve our thinking around.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Certainly some of the things that we focus on at a very rudimentary level is we want the system to be up.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: You know, when you try to log into it, it's responsive to you and you can log into it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: In preparing for this, we took a look back.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The system was up 99.1% of the time, or even more than that.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So the system wasn't out.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It wasn't down.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So that's certainly positive.

chapters.summary: Yu reports 35,330 registered contracts, 22,605 amendments, $187B contract value, $27B amendment value, 472,000 invoices dispersed, 135,000 invoices created in FY26, and about 87,000 users last year.
chapters.title: Yu lists PASSPort volume metrics

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The other thing that we track, and that's on the technology itself.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The other thing that we are continuing to count

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I'll rattle off some stats.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So to date, the number of registered contracts is 35,330.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The number of amendments, 22,605.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Overall contract value on those, $187 billion.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The amendment value, $27 billion.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The number of invoices dispersed, $472,000.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: For fiscal year 26, the number of invoices created, $135,000, and that's a 12% increase over FY25.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So we certainly see that the workload of the city of New York is being supported in the system.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We're also tracking on the number of vendors who are in the system, number of agencies who are in the system.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The number of vendors filed is about 34,000.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The number of active agency users, 123,000.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And we see that the traffic in the system, about 87,000 used the system last year.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So those are some of the metrics.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And those are around the technology itself.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And I will say...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: What is more important to me is some of the things we were speaking about earlier, on-time contract registration, on-time payment, and the technology should be supportive of the business.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: That's priority.

chapters.summary: Restler says the system processes remarkable activity but questions whether it works as efficiently as it should and meets multiple needs; he appreciates the data points.
chapters.title: Restler comments on PASSPort effectiveness and efficiency

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's helpful.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I mean, I think that broadly, it's,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: the system works, we're processing a phenomenal amount of activity through it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's just, I think, the question of, like, does it work as efficiently as it should, and does it meet our multiplicity of needs as efficiently as it should?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So, but I appreciate that it is effective, and we are executing on the things that we need to as a city, and the data points that you just referenced are quite remarkable.

chapters.summary: Restler asks whether DOE consulted MOCS before procuring a separate system; Yu says she knew of conversations, prior attempts to bring DOE into PASSPort stalled on governance questions, and DOE has space to modernize.
chapters.title: Restler asks about DOE's separate procurement system

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Just briefly on DOE kind of announcing a new procurement system, did they consult with you and the MOX team on this decision to procure a separate contract rather than finally adopting Passport or becoming a Passport user?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I certainly knew of those conversations.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: There were some prior conversations in the last administration of potentially having DOE come into passport.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: At that time,

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: there were some governance questions that we, there will always continue to be governance conversations around the technology solutions serving the mayoral agencies versus DOE.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And we did not resolve those governance issues.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I do understand or do have knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: there's some space to modernize the procurement and contracting systems at DOE.

chapters.summary: Restler says DOE is the biggest city agency and wishes the city were on the same page rather than DOE operating in its own silo.
chapters.title: Restler wishes city and DOE worked together on procurement systems

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yeah, I just wish that we were all working together on the same page on it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: They're the biggest agency in the city, and it just...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If they're going to be taking a whole new direction, did it make sense for the city as a whole to take a direction with them?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Or are they going to continue to kind of operate in their own silo?

chapters.summary: Restler asks about ballot question 2, which would let the Procurement Policy Board set vendor questionnaire contents and reduce paperwork for small vendors; Yu supports a tailored, risk-based approach after 30 years.
chapters.title: Restler asks about ballot question 2 and vendor questionnaire

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And then I just briefly would like to ask about the ballot question since they feel timely.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Ballot question two.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: has several measures that would impact MOX.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It would let the Procurement Policy Board set the contents of the vendor questionnaire and allow certain vendors, like small businesses, to file less paperwork.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Good thing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Can you expand on what impact this would have on vendors?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And if approved, how would MOX implement this?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So, Chair, thank you for raising this because Election Day is around the corner and early voting is already opened.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So on this particular question.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Have you voted yet?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I have not voted yet.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I'm waiting to get my sticker on actual Election Day.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You're not doing more research onto the ballot questions.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's not the outstanding piece.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I'm going to follow all the social media on it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Well, maybe your testimony today will help educate people about question two and whether they should support it.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So on that, overall.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The procurement rules and the policies, it's been a collection and layer upon layer.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And often what happens is something bad will happen in the contracting space and in the procurement space.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And folks will, with well intentions, will put a policy in place that served a purpose for a particular set of circumstances and a particular time and place.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: However, what the government and we all struggle with is doing a look back.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And does that still serve us?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Something that was put in place 10 years ago, 20 years ago, 30 years ago.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I want to say that the VENDEX or the vendor questionnaire, the principal questionnaire, it's probably been around for 30 years, if not more.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: So it is time for us to take another look.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And it just makes sense that we are not a one-size-fits-all approach.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: There are lots of different organizations that contract with the city of New York, and it does make sense to have a little bit more of a tailored approach and different risk allocation measures for what we're seeing in the contracting activity.

chapters.summary: Restler asks how many contracts over $5M without competitive bidding would be affected by delegating approval to agency chief contracting officers; Yu says she will provide numbers, guesses thousands, and says delegation is not abdication.
chapters.title: Restler asks about delegation of contracts over $5M

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And the proposal would allow the mayor to delegate to agency chief contracting officers, to ACCOs, the approval of contracts over $5 million that are awarded without competitive bidding, which the mayor cannot delegate today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The commission estimated that the delegation could save one to two weeks on a procurement.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you have an estimate of how many contracts this would impact?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Like how many contracts we're looking at that are over $5 million without a competitive process?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And if approval is delegated to an ACCO, what role would MOX play in reviewing those contracts?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I can come back with the number.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: The number is not great.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's not large.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I think it's in the thousands.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Oh, you think thousands of contracts over $5 million without a competitive process?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Maybe depending on the year.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But we can provide some numbers.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We can look back and provide some numbers.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I would have guessed smaller.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: What did you guess?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I guessed it was...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Molly, what did you think?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Molly doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I would have guessed a couple hundred.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: A couple hundred.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: You may be closer.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: But.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And when we're confronted with this question around delegations, and this applies to question number two, but then even beyond, delegation is not abdication.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Delegation is a controlled...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Tool to allow some things to move based upon the circumstances, we will still retain oversight and we will still try to ensure the accountability.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: We'll do spot checks and the other thing is we always want to position our agency chief contracting officers well and we do that through professional development and we will still maintain that.

chapters.summary: Restler asks about making public comment permanent in place of hearings and raising the value threshold for public comment; Yu agrees with the estimated 30-day savings and says hearings are held less than once a month, often for shelter contracts.
chapters.title: Restler asks about public comment replacing hearings

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The proposal would also make permanent the use of a public comment period in place of a public hearing for contract awards and would allow the Procurement Policy Board to raise the contract value that requires public comment

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: beginning in 2030.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The Commission estimated that the proposal's reforms

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: together could save up to 30 days on a procurement.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you agree with that estimate?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And how often are hearings currently held now?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I do agree with it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Was it your estimate?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: No, it was not my estimate.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I appreciate that, though.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I also...

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Going back to sort of my earlier point about procurement being this collection of things that have evolved over the passage of time, public hearing, public comment have had their moment in time.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And so much of what we do now, putting information publicly available on the website, sort of satiates this public notice.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: And so doing away with some of the more rigid requirements that exist in the charter, those are all welcomed sort of evolution of and modernizing procurement and contracting.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And just tell me again, how often are these hearings held?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's more than once a month?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: I think it's less than once a month.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Oh, really?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It's less than once a month, but we will come back.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Does anyone ever come?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: It depends on the time.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Mostly for the shelter?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Contracts?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's for the shelter contracts people show up in less for other stuff?

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Or a particular procurement that happens to be controversial as much as that happens.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Because I felt like when I was involved in shelter setting, people would have those contracts on their radar as a way where they could just go and scream about something that they didn't like.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: A little bit of NIMBY happening.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Kim Yu
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You okay?

chapters.summary: Restler thanks Yu for her testimony and says the committee appreciates the informative conversation.
chapters.title: Restler thanks Director Yu and concludes administration testimony

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that that covers all of our questions for the day.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you for making yourself available and for your thoughtful answers.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I think the informative conversation, we really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So thank you so much, Director Yu.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm good.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Restler opens the public testimony period, reminds the public of decorum, explains sign-up and the three-minute speaking limit, gives instructions for written testimony, and calls Charles Diamond and Jessie Faye Parrott.
chapters.title: Restler opens public testimony and calls first panel

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I have to now read something out loud that says, in advance of a public comment period, I just need to find my notes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Here we go.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I now open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and the decorum should be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: As such, members of the public should remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant of Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out a peer's card with the Sergeant of Arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have three minutes to speak on today's hearing topic.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If you have written a statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant of Arms.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimonycouncil.nmc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We will now call up the first panel, which in...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Charles Diamond, and online we have somebody else, and they can testify as well, Jesse Faye Parrott.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you both.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We'll start with Mr.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Diamond and then go online.

chapters.summary: Charles Diamond argues the city spends about $40B annually through PASSPort but only about $10M on maintenance, urges more investment in MOCS and agency staffing, criticizes DOE's separate system, and supports ballot question 2.
chapters.title: Charles Diamond testifies on PASSPort spending and reform

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Hello, good afternoon, Chair, to the entire Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: How are you doing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat a stat you've heard me say many times before, but regarding how much we're spending on Passport and given what we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: We talk about, I think, $40 billion annually is a good estimate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: This year is with the report that was just released was 36.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: The year before that, we're closer to 45.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: $40 billion annually, and our benchmark is $10 million for maintenance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: The total OTPS spending for MOX, the only agency responsible for any of the spending on Passport, is $14 million this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: That's down from $22 million the year before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: As I said it before, we're not going to get better procurement outcomes unless we invest in it and we actually care about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I think Director Yu spoke incredibly honestly and powerfully about maintaining the system and the importance of doing that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: But you also mentioned the list, which I think we've all seen at various different times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: It is very long.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: We know what to do, and I would really urge the council to get the administration to take this more seriously, where they're going to put the money,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: not just into MOX, but also into the staffing at the different agencies, into more dynamic standardization, into the change in management that that requires, not just spending on Passport.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: So really, I just wanted to point out once again the disparity between...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: What we're asking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: asking the system to do, which is $40 billion a year of transactions, and what we're willing to spend to maintain it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: So I think we need to be realistic about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: In particular, we talk about these persistent problems that have not gone away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I want to bring up a couple of things that came up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: You mentioned the DOE collaboration, of course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: We've been going through a kind of 2019 history time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I remember back then as well, when I was with the controller's office, there was an agreement made based off of some DOE scandals that DOE would work closely with MOX and basically take a lot of MOX advice and do things like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: That and...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: DOE would send some money to MOX to observe that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: That's even before the potential incorporation into Passport.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Those efforts are clearly no longer there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: And I think when we see a DOE again saying, we're bringing every resource to bear, we're going to create a new system, these are problems that we've known about for a very, very, very long time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: So I do think connecting the issues of how much are we spending to support procurement versus what's going on at DOE is very important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: It would be scary if they end up spending $25 million on a solution when we're not willing to spend that on something that's the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Ballot proposal number two, briefly, I would mention with the public hearings process, I was part of the team that made that happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Back in the day, we got public comment on less than 1% of all contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: That was the official line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: My estimate, which I testified to the state legislature of many, many years ago, was 25 days that we saved by going to online notice and comment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Compared to the old process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: But it's what we're doing right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: We have to do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I certainly think everyone should vote yes onto their fantastic proposals across the board.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I would note, Chair Ressler, on the idea of the approvals, I would, of those contracts over $5 million, as I've mentioned in other hearings as well, that's a bit of a red herring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: That all, frankly, can all be done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: The really, really most fantastic thing, I think, is mandatory quarterly meetings for the Procurement Policy Board, which will really make sure that we can't ignore reform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Restler notes the administration could already hold more Procurement Policy Board hearings without a charter amendment, but says mandating quarterly meetings is welcome.
chapters.title: Restler responds on PPB quarterly meetings

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I will note on the record that it's up to the administration to choose to have as many criminal policy board hearings as they want.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: They don't need a ballot amendment to charter revision, a charter amendment to to have quarterly meetings, but mandating it is a welcome thing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And with that, I will kick it to Jesse Faye Parrott online.

chapters.summary: Jessie Faye Parrott of the Human Services Council says PASSPort has chronic delays, lacks an accessible interface, forces providers to use multiple systems, and blocks invoices during budget mods, causing financial strain and program closures.
chapters.title: Jessie Faye Parrott testifies on nonprofit PASSPort burdens

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Welcome, Jesse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Hi, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Chair and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Thank you so much for having me today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: My name is Jessie Faye Parrott, and I'm a policy analyst at the Human Services Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: We are a membership organization representing over 180 human services providers across the state.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: HSC serves as an advocate and intermediary between the sector and the government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: We take on this work so that our members can focus on providing critical direct support for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Historically, the procurement process has been rife for nonprofits with chronic delays that cost significant time and money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Passport is no different with chronic delays at every step of the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Passport lacks an accessible user interface and many providers report preferring HHS Accelerator for its accessibility and design in partnership with the sector.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: The nonprofit provider is the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: the end user of Passport and should be part of the conversation in fixing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: There is no centralized city policy on agency use of Passport and information management.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Some agencies use other systems in addition to Passport, such as DYCD Connect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Doubling document submission time is a significant burden on providers who are already stretched very thin when they have to work in more than one online platform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Issues with Passport also put financial strain on nonprofit providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: In Passport, once you submit a budget mod, you can no longer submit invoices until the mod is approved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: I know that Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Yu spoke about this earlier, and I really appreciate the upcoming release of Passport 7.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: However, this is not a city procurement policy, but a quirk of passport.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Providers are put in impossible positions having to choose when to submit budget mods as that will directly impact their cash flow, since they are not able to invoice for however long the budget mod approval takes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: These delays pile up and providers can be owed years of retroactive budget add-ons like the COLA and indirect cost rates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: The city has promised to fix this issue and has yet to roll out a solution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: But hopefully soon I will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Late payments to providers are not an accounting hiccup.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: When reimbursement lags by months or even years, providers cannot respond to crises and end up in crisis themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: As providers take on debt to meet needs when the city doesn't pay, staff burn out and programs close.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Although the city has taken on reform efforts to address the procurement challenges that nonprofits face, the primary technological infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: in the procurement process is inaccessible, inefficient, and contributes to massive delays.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Thank you for providing me with this opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: I am looking forward to working further with you to support our life-saving essential human services providers, and I'm happy to take any questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessie Faye Parrott
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Restler thanks Charles Diamond and Jessie Faye Parrott for testifying, wishes them a good afternoon, and adjourns the hearing.
chapters.title: Restler thanks public witnesses and adjourns hearing

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really appreciate you both taking the time to testify today and share your insights and expertise.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It is greatly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I wish we had a few more people here to share their opinions about Passport, but I really appreciate each of yours.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So thank you both for taking the time today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Hope you both have a great afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And with that, I am going to adjourn this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Actually, the Sergeant at Arms.

summary: The Committee on Contracts held an oversight hearing on PASSPort, the city's procurement and sourcing portal, with testimony from MOCS Director Kim Yu and DDC Commissioner Paul Ochoa.

Council members questioned PASSPort costs, contract renewals, nonprofit invoice burdens, reporting limitations, capital project tracking, and four bills on small capital project design, timeframes, and cost benchmarks plus Reso 619 on design-build.
Public witnesses Charles Diamond and Jessie Faye Parrott criticized PASSPort spending and nonprofit burdens, and Chair Restler adjourned after testimony.
